summary: `recentWindow`'s paging loop is guarded by `collected.length < limit`. With `limit` 0 or NaN the guard is false on entry, so the walk executes ZERO pages: `collected` is empty, `tailToken` is undefined, `exhaustedTheTimeline` is false and `stale` is false, so control falls through to `emptyWindowCursor(undefined, undefined, false)` — which mints the bare `@parley-stream:` sentinel meaning "the first visible event in the room". This is precisely the position `cursor.ts` and `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts` go to great lengths to make unmintable for a room that has history; the zero/NaN-limit path reaches it by never looking at a page at all.
failure: post(t,'a'); post(t,'b'); post(t,'c'); then `fetchRecent({topic: t, limit: 0})` (or `limit: NaN`) -> `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '@parley-stream:' }`. Replaying that cursor returns ['a','b','c'] — the whole room. Core's catch-up persists whatever cursor it is handed, so the next start re-drains the room into agent context with a fresh seen-set; in `shared_room` mode that is every topic's history. Reproduced with a probe test.
remediation: Normalize `limit` at the seam entry the way `blockMs` already is (index.ts:114): `const asked = args.limit ?? 100; const limit = Number.isInteger(asked) && asked > 0 ? asked : 100;`. Fixing it inside `recentWindow` (e.g. treating a zero-page walk as a short circuit) is worse — a since-less read has no caller position to fall back on and would have to throw for a legitimate `limit: 0`.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a read that executed no page may not report a position no walk observed. Extend `degenerate-block-budget.fake.test.ts` — whose LIMIT_ROWS already carry 0, NaN and Infinity but assert only settlement and request cost — to assert, for every cell against a provisioned room, `String(res.nextCursor) !== '@parley-stream:'` and that `drainFrom(q, t, res.nextCursor)` returns only what the call did not deliver. That is the same predicate `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts` applies to the short-circuit table; widening it to the degenerate-argument table makes the two tables grade one invariant instead of two disjoint halves of it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `const limit = args.limit ?? 100;` (index.ts:122) and the two paging guards it feeds: `messages.length < limit` (drainForward) and `collected.length < limit` (recentWindow).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `limit: 0` / `limit: NaN` / `limit: -3` now read the newest 100 messages instead of returning an empty page. A caller who literally meant "zero" gets 100 — astonishing, but the seam has no error channel and core's own tool schema already rejects non-positive limits, so nothing in the shipped stack asks for zero.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — nothing throws that did not before.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the fix and ran degenerate-block-budget (120 cells), recent-window-and-cursor and catchup-sync: 336 tests, all green. The degenerate table staying green under the fix is direct evidence its `limit` axis grades nothing about the cursor.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the underlying `recentWindow` behaviour stays, a zero-page walk can still mint `@parley-stream:` from any OTHER route that reaches it with a falsy-guard limit (none today, but `blockingFetch` and the 404 fallback both call `recentWindow` with a `limit` they receive rather than derive). Belt-and-braces would also make `recentWindow` refuse to claim a position when `page === 0`.

summary: `validateConfig` checks `shared_room` only for "a non-empty string". `roomLocalpart` then returns it VERBATIM (`this.sharedLocalpart ?? boundedLocalpart(topic, this.serverName)`), so it bypasses both guards the derived path has: the `sanitizeAlias` charset fold and the `MAX_ALIAS_BYTES` bound. `validateConfig`'s own docstring says these must be LOAD ERRORS "the way `skip_permissions: true` is", and `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` asserts `ALIAS_LEGAL = /^#[A-Za-z0-9._-]+:[^:]+$/` for every derived alias — a predicate the operator-supplied one never meets.
failure: `shared_room: 'a:b'` is accepted at load and produces the alias `#a:b:fake`, which Matrix parses by splitting on the FIRST colon: localpart `a`, server-name `b:fake` — a different server than `server_name` configures. `shared_room: '#hash'` produces `##hash:fake`; `'ok/slash'` produces `#ok/slash:fake`; `'x'.repeat(400)` produces a 400+ byte alias past the 255-byte limit `boundedLocalpart` exists to enforce. All four reproduced. Every one fails later as an opaque homeserver 400 that names neither the plugin nor the config key, and per alias.ts's own comment an over-long alias makes the deployment "silently never work": `post` rejects with the homeserver's 400 while every read returns the empty page an unwritten topic returns.
remediation: In `validateConfig`, after the non-empty-string check, reject `shared_room` unless `/^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$/.test(cfg.shared_room)` and `Buffer.byteLength('#' + cfg.shared_room + ':' + (cfg.server_name ?? 'parley.local'), 'utf8') <= 255`, with a message naming the charset and the byte budget. Note `validateConfig` runs before `this.serverName` is assigned, so the server name must be read off `cfg`, not off the instance.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every backend name the plugin puts on the wire — derived OR operator-supplied — satisfies the same legality predicate. Move `ALIAS_LEGAL` and the 255-byte bound out of `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` into a shared helper and drive `config-validation.test.ts`'s `shared_room` row from it: a parameterized rejected-set of {' ', '#', ':', '/', '�', a 400-char run, an emoji} plus a generator that fuzzes localparts and asserts "accepted at load" iff "matches ALIAS_LEGAL and fits the budget". Today `shared_room.rejected` holds only `true` and `''`.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `reject(key, expected, why)` in config.ts:97, which reads `cfg[key]` and throws `backend_config.shared_room = ... is not accepted` — the shape `config-validation.test.ts` matches with `new RegExp('backend_config\\.' + field)`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `shared_room` values containing anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, and any value whose `#<localpart>:<server_name>` exceeds 255 bytes. `'a:b'`, `'#hash'`, `'ok/slash'` and 400-char runs stop loading.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. Every `shared_room` value the repo actually uses passes the new predicate: `'parley_conformance'` (config-validation accepted row, fake-synapse SHARED_LOCALPART), `'parley_all'` (creds-warning), `'parley_conformance_YYYYMMDD'` (conformance.test.ts dailyRoom), and `PARLEY_MATRIX_SHARED_ROOM` is unset in CI. I did not run the suite with this change applied, so this is a read of the fixtures rather than an observation.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It closes the load-time hole. It does not touch the OTHER operator-supplied name on the same wire, `server_name`, which is still only checked for non-emptiness and is concatenated into every alias — a `server_name` containing `:` or `#` produces the same class of malformed alias through the derived path, and `boundedLocalpart` only budgets its BYTES, never its charset.

summary: `readRetryAfter` returns the `Retry-After` header as soon as it parses one and never reads `retry_after_ms`. But net-util already reads the header itself and combines the two with `Math.max(header, parsed ?? 0)` (index.ts:158), so returning the header collapses that max to `max(h, h) = h` and the body hint is unreachable whenever a header exists. net-util's `retryAfterOf` contract is explicit: "A source of an ADDITIONAL hint, never a ceiling... Do not clamp what you return here, so that a parser bug cannot retry sooner than the vendor asked." This module's own docstring claims the opposite outcome — "so that we never retry sooner than the homeserver asked" — which is false in exactly this case.
failure: A 429 carrying `Retry-After: 1` and `{"retry_after_ms": 5000}` -> `readRetryAfter` returns 1000 (reproduced), so `fetchWithRetry` waits 1000ms and re-sends 4 seconds inside the window the homeserver asked us to stay out of — the escalation-to-a-ban path net-util's comment names. Synapse itself currently ceils the header so it is latent there; a gateway that emits its own coarser `Retry-After`, or a non-Synapse homeserver (Dendrite/Conduit) that floors it, reaches it.
remediation: Delete the header branch from `readRetryAfter` and return only the body's `retry_after_ms`; let `fetchWithRetry` take the max of that and the header it already parses. The same shape is present in bridge-discord/rest.ts:68, bridge-telegram/wire.ts:187 and bridge-zulip/wire.ts:117 — this is a cross-package theme, not a Matrix instance.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a per-backend `retryAfterOf` may only ADD to the header floor. Replace `rate-limit.fake.test.ts`'s `'both present — the header wins'` row (which pins the bug) with a parameterized table over the cross product {header absent, header < body, header == body, header > body} x {body absent, body present} asserting the EFFECTIVE wait observed through `fetchWithRetry` (with an injected clock) rather than `readRetryAfter`'s return value — the unit under test is the combination, and grading the hook alone is what let the narrowing look correct. Then run the same table against every backend that ships a `retryAfterOf`.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `fetchWithRetry` index.ts:156-158: `const header = usableHint(retryAfterFromHeader(res)); const parsed = usableHint(await callerHint(opts.retryAfterOf, res)); const hinted = header === undefined ? parsed : Math.max(header, parsed ?? 0);` — the max branch is what makes dropping the header branch safe.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A 429 with `Retry-After: 1` + `retry_after_ms: 5000` now waits 5000ms instead of 1000ms.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at the transport level. But a 429 whose stated wait now exceeds `deadlineMs` ends the call with `upstream asked for Nms, past this call's ...ms deadline` where it previously retried — for a Synapse-shaped 45s createRoom limit that is already the shipped behaviour, so no new class of failure.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: THREE rows of `rate-limit.fake.test.ts` > 'the 429 hint the retry loop is handed': 'Retry-After header in seconds' (expects 45000, would get undefined), 'Retry-After header as an HTTP-date' (predicate on ~40000, would get undefined), 'both present — the header wins' (expects 7000, would get 1000). All three grade `readRetryAfter` in isolation, which is the wrong unit; they must be re-pointed at the combined hint. I did not run them under the change.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken, but the fix is invisible while the three unit rows above still exist — they will fail loudly, and 'restore the header branch' is the tempting wrong response.

summary: `FakeSynapse` captures `Authorization` into `requestAuth` and its docstring says "Keep the credential observable, so that WHICH token went to WHICH homeserver is gradeable: a plugin that carries one login's bearer token to another host is indistinguishable from a healthy one on the URL alone." But no endpoint ever CHECKS it. Every path except `/v3/login` serves the same 200 whether the request carries the right bearer, the wrong host's bearer, or none. Only `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts` inspects `requestAuth`, and only for the login and the post-reconnect happy path — so the entire authenticated surface of the plugin is graded solely by whether a URL was hit.
failure: Mutate `session.ts:334` from `if (this.token !== undefined) headers.Authorization = ...` to a no-op (the plugin sends no bearer anywhere) and every fake-driven file in the package stays green: 18 files, ~890 tests. That is a mutation which, against a real homeserver, makes the plugin 401 on literally every call. It is also why finding #1 (unauthenticated requests after `disconnect()`) is invisible offline and passes the frozen conformance clause on the strength of Synapse's own 401.
remediation: Have `FakeSynapse.fetch` answer 401 `{errcode:'M_MISSING_TOKEN'}` for any non-`/v3/login` request whose `Authorization` is not `bearerFor(url.host)`, and add a directed case asserting that the mutation above turns the suite red.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a fixture that RECORDS a security-relevant property must also ENFORCE it, or the property is graded only where a test happens to read the recording. Add a fixture self-test to `fake-synapse.ts`'s consumers — a table of {no header, wrong host's bearer, malformed bearer} x {directory, join, state, send, messages, context, sync} asserting each is refused — so a new endpoint added to the fake without an auth check fails the day it lands. Generalize the same audit to the other backends' fakes: any header a fake stores in a public field and never branches on is a claim it cannot support.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `const auth = new Headers(init?.headers).get('authorization') ?? undefined;` (fake-synapse.ts:321) and `bearerFor(host)` (line 589), both already present.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any fake-driven request the plugin makes without the current host's bearer. That includes the post-teardown requests finding #1 describes, and the send-idempotency map's `txnKey = auth + '|' + txn`, which already keys on auth.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Unknown — I did not run the suite with the fake tightened. `provisioning.fake.test.ts`'s SIDE_EFFECTS table and `reconnect-lifecycle`'s teardown table both drive calls that straddle a `disconnect()` (which clears the token), so some of those rows would start seeing 401s where they see 200s today. That is arguably the correct new behaviour, but it means this remediation is a suite-wide change, not a one-line fixture edit.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Enforcing auth makes the mutation detectable but does not by itself fix finding #1 — the plugin would then reject after teardown for the wrong reason (a 401 from the fixture) rather than refusing to talk. Both changes are needed for the class to be closed.

summary: `ensureRoom`'s failure handler is `this.rooms.delete(key)` with no generation check, while `standDown()` clears `this.rooms` wholesale. A promise started under generation N that rejects AFTER a reconnect therefore evicts generation N+1's entry for the same key.
failure: gen 1: `post(t)` sets `rooms['t'] = P1`. `connect()` -> `standDown()` clears `rooms`. gen 2: `post(t)` sets `rooms['t'] = P2`. P1 now rejects (reachable: `fetchWithRetry` throws `<label> -> 429 (disconnected)` once `isStopped` turns true, or `joinRoom` 403s) -> its `.catch` deletes `rooms['t']`, i.e. P2. P2 still resolves for its own caller, but the cache is empty, so the next `post`/`existingRoom` on that topic pays a fresh `/directory` lookup + `/join` + `/state` round-trip it should not have needed.
remediation: Capture `const generation = this.generation` in `ensureRoom` and make the cleanup conditional: `if (this.rooms.get(key) === pending) this.rooms.delete(key);` — identity on the promise is stronger than a generation check and also covers the intra-generation case.
testUpgrade: CLASS: cleanup on a cache keyed by a value a teardown clears must be identity-scoped, not key-scoped. Parameterize a case over {ensureRoom via post, ensureRoom via subscribe} x {rejection arrives before the reconnect, after it} asserting that the number of `/directory` lookups after the reconnect is exactly one per distinct topic — an assertion that would also catch the same shape in `existingRoom`'s `rooms.set` if that ever grows a cleanup path.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `const pending = this.resolveOrCreateRoom(...).catch(...); this.rooms.set(key, pending);` (session.ts:120-125). The identity test requires `pending` to be the value stored, which it is.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no call's outcome changes, only whether a cache entry survives.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. No test asserts a cache MISS after a reconnect; `reconnect-lifecycle`'s registry table asserts `rooms.size === 0` after teardown, which the identity guard does not affect (the entry there is deleted by `standDown`'s `clear()`, not by the catch). Untested — I did not run it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken; the symptom is one extra round-trip. If the bug remained, the fix would simply not fire.
remediationCheck.interleavings: P1 rejects while P2 is pending (evicts P2); P1 rejects after P2 resolves (evicts a resolved entry); two callers entering `ensureRoom` in the same tick under gen 2 — the second sees P2 in the map and shares it, so the identity guard is still correct for it.

summary: `MatrixPlugin extends MatrixParking extends MatrixTimeline extends MatrixSession` is a four-level inheritance chain in which no level declares an abstract member, nothing is overridden anywhere, and each `abstract class` has exactly one descendant. The `abstract` keyword carries no contract — it only says "do not instantiate". The chain exists solely to split one 1,150-line class across four files, and the price is that ~12 pieces of mutable state (`token`, `baseUrl`, `rooms`, `controllers`, `waiters`, `liveTopics`, `stopped`, `generation`, ...) are `protected` and reachable from any of the four with no declared surface between them.
failure: Not a runtime failure. The concrete cost is visible in the tests: five test files reach into the plugin through `p as unknown as { waiters: Map<...>; controllers: Set<...>; liveTopics: Set<string>; rooms: Map<...>; token: string }` because there is no seam to assert against — the exact cast-through-a-private-member shape CLAUDE.md's architectural-tests rule names as a failure mode, and the reason a renamed field would silently turn those assertions into `expect(undefined).toBeUndefined()`.
remediation: Convert the chain to composition: keep the four files, but make `MatrixSession` a plain class the others HOLD rather than extend, and give each layer an explicit constructor-injected interface. Drop `abstract` where it declares nothing. This is a refactor with no behaviour change, so it belongs behind the same green suite rather than in a fix round with anything else.
testUpgrade: CLASS: an assertion that reaches private state through a cast cannot survive a rename. Replace the five `p as unknown as {...}` casts with a single exported test-observation surface (e.g. an `internalCounts()` method or a symbol-keyed accessor) and add one case asserting that surface names every registry `standDown()` clears — derived from `Object.keys` of the surface rather than from the hand-written `REGISTRIES` literal in `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts`, so a registry added later is graded the day it appears instead of the day someone remembers to extend the array.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `grep -n 'abstract|override|extends' src/*.ts` returns only the three class declarations and zero member-level `abstract`/`override` — verified.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — behaviour-preserving by construction.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Every file holding a `p as unknown as {...}` cast to a protected field: blocking-fetch-cleanup, reconnect-lifecycle, provisioning, recent-window-and-cursor, live-per-topic. They would need re-pointing at whatever observation surface replaces the casts, which is the point of the change rather than collateral. Untested — I did not attempt the refactor.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; this trades a latent maintainability and test-fragility cost for a mechanical refactor. If the refactor were done badly (state duplicated across the composed objects instead of owned by one), it would introduce a real bug where none exists — which is why it should land alone.

summary: The table is 5 blockMs x 4 limit x 3 since x 2 provisioned = 120 cells, each doing a login, a seed, a fetch and a replay. Its three assertions are `observed.status === 'resolved'`, a request-count ceiling keyed only on `blockMs`, and a replay done with a hard-coded `limit: 50`. Nothing in any of them can differ across the four `limit` rows — the axis costs 90 cells of runtime and cannot independently fail. The one property the `limit` axis WOULD discriminate is the cursor the degenerate limit mints, and that is exactly the defect it lets through (see the `@parley-stream:` finding): I applied the limit-normalization fix and all 120 cells stayed green.
failure: Run the file with `LIMIT_ROWS` reduced to `[['default', undefined]]` — 30 cells instead of 120 — and the suite grades precisely as much as it does today, minus the ~90 cells of wall clock. Conversely, changing `const limit = args.limit ?? 100` to `const limit = 100` (deleting the caller's limit entirely) leaves all 120 cells green.
remediation: Either give the `limit` axis an assertion it can fail — `expect(String(res.nextCursor)).not.toBe('@parley-stream:')` for the provisioned rows, and `expect(res.messages.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(limit)` for the finite ones — or delete the axis and let `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts`'s CAP_LIMITS table own `limit` entirely.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every axis of a cartesian test table must be able to change an assertion. Add a meta-check to the package's lint file (`comment-hygiene.test.ts` is the existing home for package-local rules): for each `describe` built from nested loops, assert that at least one `expect` in the body references the loop variable. Failing that, the cheap durable version is to make each degenerate row assert the cursor AND the page cap as functions of `limit`, so a row that cannot distinguish itself from its neighbours fails to compile a distinct expectation.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `const budgeted = Number.isFinite(blockMs) && blockMs > 0;` and `expect(spent).toBeLessThanOrEqual(budgeted ? 24 : 6)` — the only assertion that reads a loop variable, and it reads `blockMs`, never `limit`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: n/a
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Adding the cursor assertion turns 30 cells RED against the current code — that is the intended demonstration for the `@parley-stream:` finding, not collateral. Adding it AFTER the limit-normalization fix leaves the file green (verified: I ran the file with the fix applied, 120/120 passed).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Deleting the axis without adding the cursor assertion would REMOVE the only place the degenerate inputs are exercised at all, so the two halves of this remediation must land together or the fix half must land first.

summary: onStanza dispatches ANY <message> carrying a <result xmlns='urn:xmpp:mam:2'> child to the MAM-collector path and returns, before it looks at stanza type or at who sent it. A MUC reflects an occupant's own unknown children verbatim, so a co-occupant can attach that child to its own groupchat message: the message is then never seen by onGroupchat, so it is neither delivered to subscribers nor used to fire the long-poll waiters — while it IS in the MAM archive, so the live and catch-up paths disagree. The sibling guard in onMamResult compares only jid.bareOf(from) to the queried room, so a `<result>` from an occupant JID (room@svc/eve) passes provenance; onErrorMessage next door explicitly requires resourceOf(from) === '' for exactly this reason.
failure: Against a real Prosody (parley-critic-xmpp-8e8, examples/dev-compose config): plugin.subscribe(topic); a second account joins the room and sends `<message to='room@muc.parley.local' type='groupchat'><body>hostile</body><result xmlns='urn:xmpp:mam:2' queryid='x'/></message>`. Observed LIVE handler contents ['seed','benign'] — 'hostile' absent — while fetchRecent returned ['seed','benign','hostile']. Same input against FakeXmpp: a fetchRecent({since: tail, blockMs: 1500}) with that stanza delivered at 60 ms returned an EMPTY page after 1502 ms instead of waking on the message.
remediation: In onStanza, take the MAM-result branch only for a stanza that is a plausible MAM envelope: require stanza.attrs.type === undefined (a MAM <result> is carried on a typeless <message>) and pass the FULL from to onMamResult; in onMamResult require jid.resourceOf(from) === '' && jid.bareOf(from) === collector.room, mirroring onErrorMessage's 'a service stanza always comes from the BARE room JID (RFC 6120 §8.3)' guard. Do not `return` from onStanza on a stanza that failed the MAM test — let it fall through to the type='groupchat' arm so a message with a junk child is still delivered.
testUpgrade: Generalise live-field-provenance.test.ts's `children` table from {<delay>,<stanza-id>} to EVERY child an occupant can attach that the plugin's dispatcher or parser reads: add `<result xmlns='urn:xmpp:mam:2'>`, `<forwarded xmlns='urn:xmpp:forward:0'>`, `<origin-id xmlns='urn:xmpp:sid:0'>` and `<error>`, and add a second assertion axis to each row: 'the message is still delivered on the live path AND still wakes a parked long-poll'. Today the table only asserts that a forged VALUE is not honoured, so a child that makes the whole message vanish satisfies every row. Drive the same table through both the FakeXmpp arm and the gated real-MUC arm at the bottom of that file. mam-provenance.test.ts's 'keeps the legitimate one' row must be re-pointed at outerFrom = the BARE room JID (it currently uses `${ROOM}/alice`, which certifies the weak check).

remediationCheck.reliesOn: inbound.ts onStanza's existing `if (!stanza.is('message')) return;` and the `stanza.attrs.type === 'error' / 'groupchat'` arms below it; jid.resourceOf/bareOf; the precedent guard in onErrorMessage `if (jid.resourceOf(from) !== '') return;`. Prosody's own MAM results were observed in this run arriving on a typeless <message> from the bare room JID, which is the branch the fix keeps taking.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A groupchat message from a co-occupant that carries a stray <result xmlns='urn:xmpp:mam:2'> child: it now reaches onGroupchat, is delivered to subscribers, and fires the room's long-poll waiters.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A <result xmlns='urn:xmpp:mam:2'> whose outer stanza carries a type attribute, or whose from carries a resource (room@svc/eve). Both are dropped from the collector.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: mam-provenance.test.ts:56 'drops a <result> whose outer from is NOT the queried room, and keeps the legitimate one' — its 'legit' stanza uses outerFrom `${ROOM}/alice`, which the resource check now rejects, so the `expect(items).toHaveLength(1)` half goes red. mam-provenance.test.ts:91 (the negative control, outerFrom 'evil@example.com/attacker') also goes red for the same reason. Both are testing the old, weaker contract and must be re-pointed at the bare room JID. I checked the other suites for a fixture that feeds a resourced MAM result: FakeXmpp.feedMamResult already sends from the bare `room`, so archive-admission, mam-paging, long-poll-*, cursor-inputs and the conformance suite are unaffected.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the dispatcher still `return`s early on a failed MAM test, the injection is closed but the live-push suppression remains — a co-occupant's message still disappears from subscribe() and still fails to wake a blocked fetch. Both halves of the fix are needed; the fall-through is the half that closes the reproduced failure.

summary: subscribe() awaits ensureJoinedRoom(room) and only then writes into this.subscriptions. onOccupancyLost's re-entry ladder is gated on `this.subscriptions.has(room)`, so an occupancy loss delivered inside the join → assertMamAvailable(disco#info) window is classified as a catch-up-only room: forgetRoom() drops the join cache, one stderr line is printed, and NO re-join timer is armed. subscribe() then resolves successfully and registers a handler for a room the connection is not in. Live push for that topic is dead until an unrelated post()/fetchRecent() happens to re-enter the room — which for a subscribe-only topic may be never.
failure: Fake-driven probe: attach(plugin, fake); wrap fake.iqCaller.request so the disco#info probe first calls fake.endOccupancy(room, {statuses:['307']}) and then awaits 20 ms; call `await plugin.subscribe(asTopic('t-sub-race'), handler)`. subscribe resolves; observed state: joined.has(room) === false, rejoins = [['t-sub-race@muc.parley.local', losses 1, timer undefined]], stderr '[parley-xmpp] occupancy in … ended (kicked)' with no 're-joining in N ms' line. Nothing will re-enter the room.
remediation: Register the subscription BEFORE the join, and undo it if the join throws: in subscribe(), push the handler into this.subscriptions first, then `try { await this.ensureJoinedRoom(room) } catch (err) { remove this handler (and the room entry when it was the last handler); throw err }`. That makes onOccupancyLost see a subscribed room for the whole join window and arm the ladder.
testUpgrade: A parameterized case over WHEN the occupancy loss lands relative to a seam call's internal awaits — the class is 'a room-state event that arrives while the seam call that registers interest in the room is still in flight'. Table: seam call in {subscribe, post, fetchRecent} x loss-arrival point in {before the join presence is sent, after the self-presence but during the disco#info probe, after the call returns} — each cell asserting the observable 'a re-join presence for that room is sent within REJOIN_MAX_WAIT_MS'. Give FakeXmpp a `discoLatencyMs` knob so the middle point is reachable without hand-wrapping iqCaller (today only joinLatencyMs and mamLatencyMs exist, and neither covers the assertMamAvailable window). The existing membership-revalidation.test.ts rows all subscribe first and lose occupancy afterwards, so none of them can reach the window.

summary: The RISK regex /\b(?:so that|so a|so it|keep|never|cannot|can't|would|rather than|or an?\b|otherwise)\b/i is a nine-word sniff, and `or an?\b` alone matches almost any English sentence containing 'or a'. The suite's headline claim is that it grades the CLASS 'a comment that restates the code instead of warning about it', but it grades only 'the comment contains one of nine common words'. summary: validateRetentionMaxAgeNs checks the composed nanoseconds only from BELOW (`maxAgeNs < 1`). It never checks the top, so a retention_days that overflows int64 — or overflows the double — is accepted at connect() and fails, or silently inverts, at the first post. Above ~106752 days the composed max_age exceeds int64 and JetStream refuses the stream with 'invalid json'; above ~2.08e294 days Math.round yields Infinity, JSON.stringify writes `"max_age":null`, and the server stores max_age = 0 — UNLIMITED, which is precisely the outcome this function's own JSDoc says it exists to prevent.
failure: backend_config `{ retention_days: 2592000000000000 }` (a realistic unit confusion — the nanosecond value pasted into a days field) is accepted by connect() and then makes EVERY post fail: the composed max_age is 2.24e29, JSON.stringify emits exponent notation, and jsm.streams.add rejects it. Verified on nats:2.10-alpine: `streams.add({max_age: 8.64e19})` -> 'invalid json'. And `{ retention_days: 1e300 }` is accepted, composes max_age = Infinity, is serialized as `{"name":"PARLEY_retention","subjects":["parley.retention"],"max_age":null}` (printed from the fake), and on the real server `streams.add({max_age: Infinity})` returns config.max_age = 0 — retention silently unlimited and locked in at stream creation, unfixable without recreating the stream.
remediation: Add an upper bound beside the lower one in validateRetentionMaxAgeNs: `const MAX_MAX_AGE_NS = 9.223372036854775e18;` and, after `Math.round`, `if (maxAgeNs > MAX_MAX_AGE_NS) throw new Error(...)` naming retention_days and the composed nanoseconds. That single guard rejects Infinity and every finite value JetStream's int64 max_age cannot hold, at connect(), where the operator's field name is still in hand.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a value validated in the operator's unit and applied in the backend's unit, where the conversion can carry an accepted value OUT of the representable range at either end'. config.test.ts already has `boundaryDays` + the `composedMaxAge` harness and the invariant 'no accepted retention_days composes the max_age JetStream reads as unlimited' — every one of its ten rows sits at the LOW boundary (1e-15 … 1000/NS_PER_DAY), which is why this shipped. Extend the same generated table with the high side — [1e4, 1.06e5, 1.07e5, 1e6, 1e18, 1e294, 1e300, Number.MAX_VALUE] — and strengthen the invariant to: every accepted value must compose a max_age that is a finite number in [1, 2^63-1] AND must survive `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(config))` unchanged (that last clause is what catches Infinity -> null, which no numeric range assertion on the JS value can see). Keep the companion 'the boundary rows straddle the conversion' assertion so the high rows cannot all be refused or all accepted.

It calls nothing new. The consumer is streams.ts ensureStream's `if (this.retentionMaxAgeNs !== undefined) config.max_age = this.retentionMaxAgeNs;`, which is unchanged.

summary: The `restarted` predicate branches on the cursor's FORM rather than testing both conditions: a bare cursor is judged by `since.seq > lastSeq`, an incarnation-qualified one only by `since.incarnation !== this.incarnation(stream)`. So a qualified cursor naming a sequence the stream cannot have — which `since` being free caller input (`parley_fetch_recent` takes it as a plain string, as parseCursor's own JSDoc says) makes reachable — is treated as a live position: startSeq is pushed above tailSeq forever, every page is empty, and nextCursor echoes the impossible cursor straight back, so a caller that re-sends it stays deaf permanently with no error.
failure: Stream with records at seq 1,2,3 and incarnation `20260101T000000000000000Z`. `fetchRecent({topic, since: '999999'})` (bare) correctly resets and returns m1,m2,m3 with nextCursor `...Z-3`. `fetchRecent({topic, since: '20260101T000000000000000Z-999999'})` returns `messages: []` and `nextCursor: '20260101T000000000000000Z-999999'` — identical to the input — and will do so for every future call, because no message will reach seq 1000000. Reproduced by probe in the worktree.
remediation: Make the two conditions additive rather than alternative: `const restarted = since !== undefined && (since.seq > lastSeq || (since.incarnation !== undefined && since.incarnation !== this.incarnation(stream)));`. A sequence above the stream's own last_seq is impossible under ANY incarnation, so it should take the same fall-back-to-the-retained-window path the bare form already takes.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a cursor property is checked on one cursor FORM and not the other'. cursor-input.test.ts already tables read shapes × stale cursors and separately tables 'a cursor whose incarnation has grown far past / fallen short of the persisted sequence'; neither crosses form against position. Parameterize one table over form = ['bare', 'qualified-matching', 'qualified-stale'] × position = ['below first_seq', 'inside the window', 'at last_seq', 'one above last_seq', 'far above last_seq'] and assert the SAME outcome for every form at every position: a position at or below last_seq parks with the cursor it was handed, a position above last_seq reads as a cold start. That shape would also catch the inverse defect (a bare cursor at the tail wrongly resetting) which the current tables likewise cannot see.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `lastSeq = info.state.last_seq` from the StreamInfo that streamForRead/existingStream just fetched, and `this.incarnation(stream)` from the cache existingStream refreshed on the same call. It reuses the exact `since.seq > lastSeq` comparison the bare branch already performs, so it introduces no new call.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A qualified cursor whose sequence is above the stream's last_seq is now served the newest-window page (the cold-start read) instead of an empty page — i.e. the reader recovers instead of parking.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no input is rejected; one input's page changes from empty to the retained window.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I applied the change and ran the whole package suite against a real server: 1714/1714 pass. I checked cursor-input.test.ts's 'a cursor at the tail of a healthy stream still parks, and resumes on the next message' specifically: since.seq == lastSeq is not > lastSeq, so it is unaffected.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the park. The residual risk it introduces, which I traced but could not rule out by reading alone: if a fetchRecent's streams.info were ever stale relative to a just-acked post on another connection (since.seq == lastSeq+1), the read would now be judged a re-provision and served the newest `limit` messages rather than resuming — deduped by backendMsgId, but able to skip history if more than `limit` messages sat in the gap. JetStream acks a publish post-commit, so I believe streams.info cannot report a last_seq below an acked sequence, but I did not construct that race against a server. If a fix author wants to eliminate it, gate the new clause on `since.seq > lastSeq + 1`, or on the incarnation being known.

summary: `subscribe()`'s own handshake — `probeTail`'s history read (line 31) and the initial `rest.register(wire)` (line 32) — is the only pair of requests in the plugin that carries neither `conn.teardown.signal` nor a `conn.controllers` registration, so `disconnect()` cannot cut it. Every other request the loop makes is covered: the recovery re-register passes `signal` (line 161), the events poll gets its own AbortController (line 121-122), the gap-fill read gets `{ generation, signal }` (line 111), and the wake paths use `conn.deadlineAbort`. connection.ts:40 states the invariant this violates — "Aborted by `disconnect`, so a loop's in-flight history read cannot outlive its subscription" — and the subscribe handshake's history read is exactly the one that does.
failure: Reproduced against the in-process fake: `fake.hangRoute('GET /api/v1/messages')` (and separately `POST /api/v1/register`), then `plugin.subscribe(t, h)`; `await plugin.disconnect()` resolves in 209ms while the subscribe promise is STILL PENDING 6s later — it can only settle at `fetchWithRetry`'s DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS of 30_000ms. Traced consequence on the register arm: `disconnect()` returns before `register` answers, so the queue that register mints is deleted only by line 34, which runs after `close()` has already drained `pendingDeletes`; `src/cli.ts` -> `runBackendCli` calls `process.exit(0)` right after `bridge.shutdown()` (bridge-core/src/cli/backend-cli.ts:130), so a shutdown that races a slow register leaks a server-side event queue for Zulip's ~10-minute GC.
remediation: Thread the teardown signal through the handshake: `probeTail(conn, topic, generation)` should pass `{ generation, signal: conn.teardown.signal }` into `readWindow`, and line 32 should be `rest.register(wire, signal)` exactly as the recovery path at line 161 already is. Both must then map an abort to the existing diagnostic rather than letting an AbortError escape: wrap them and, when `!alive()`, throw the same 'Zulip connection was replaced while subscribe() was registering its event queue…' error the code already produces at line 35, and on the register arm still `await rest.deleteQueue(reg.queue_id)` when the register won the race.

Add a HANDSHAKE_PARK_POINTS table crossed with CONNECTION_ENDINGS, parking `subscribe()` in each round trip of its own handshake — derived from the routes a clean subscribe issues (the way blocking-fetch.test.ts derives CALL_ROUTES by observation) rather than hand-listed, so a handshake that grows a fourth request is graded the day it appears — with `fake.hangRoute(route)` for each, asserting (a) the subscribe promise settles within ~1s of `disconnect()` returning, and (b) `DELETE /api/v1/events` count >= `POST /api/v1/register` count once it settles, folding the handshake window into the existing 'releases every event queue it opens' ledger.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ZulipHttp.register(wireTopic, signal?, deadlineMs?)` already accepts a signal (http.ts:57-59) and the loop's recovery path already uses it: `const fresh = await rest.register(wire, signal)` (push-loop.ts:161). `ReadOpts` already declares `signal?: AbortSignal` and readWindow already forwards it (history.ts:46, 71). `probeTail` today calls readWindow with `{ generation }` only (history.ts:108-110), so it needs a new signal parameter.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A `subscribe()` whose handshake request is in flight when `disconnect()` lands now rejects at once instead of at the 30s transport deadline. Without the error-mapping half, it would reject with an AbortError/'This operation was aborted' instead of the crafted message.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: subscription-lifecycle.test.ts > 'no seam call answers from a connection it did not address' > the `subscribe` rows: `gradeParkedAt` holds ANY_ROUTE for 500ms, calls `entry.end(plugin, next.url)` (which runs `plugin.disconnect()`, hence `teardown.abort()`), and then asserts `expect(String(error)).toMatch(/connection was replaced/i)`. A naive signal-threading makes that reject with an abort error and those 12 rows (subscribe x 2 entries x 2 targets x up to 3 round trips) go red — which is precisely why the error-mapping half of the remediation is not optional. subscribe-race.test.ts > 'wakes on a concurrent post after disconnect raced the subscribe handshake' uses `.catch(() => undefined)` and is unaffected.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If only the `register` arm is signalled and `probeTail` is left alone, the hole stays open on the tail-probe path — my probe showed both arms hang independently. If the signal is threaded but the abort is not mapped, `disconnect()` becomes prompt but core's engine sees an opaque AbortError where the seam's own vocabulary said 'reissue it'.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Three orderings matter, and only the first is what today's code handles. (1) register answers, THEN disconnect: unchanged — `!alive()` at line 33 throws and deletes the queue. (2) disconnect, THEN register answers: today this is the 30s hang and the late delete; after the fix the register aborts and no queue is ever minted, so nothing to delete. (3) disconnect lands in the abort window while register is already committed server-side — the abort races the response; the fix must keep line 34's `await rest.deleteQueue(reg.queue_id)` on the success arm because the server may have created the queue even though the client abandoned the response. Two concurrent `subscribe()` calls on different topics share one `conn.teardown` controller, so a single `disconnect()` aborts both handshakes — that is the intended fan-out and matches how `conn.controllers` already fans out to every parked events poll.

summary: `resolveIdentity` is the one read path that trusts its declared wire types. `wire.ts:69` states the module's discipline — "Every other field is coerced rather than trusted" — and `zulipToMessage` honours it exhaustively, but `String(byEmail[0]!.user_id)` and `String(byName[0]!.user_id)` stringify whatever the server put in `user_id`, and `u?.is_active !== false` treats any non-`false` value as active. DESIGN's "inbound is untrusted" applies to `GET /api/v1/users` exactly as it does to `GET /api/v1/messages`.
failure: Reproduced with a one-member fake directory: member `{ email: 'alice@x', full_name: 'Alice' }` with no `user_id` -> `resolveIdentity('alice@x')` returns `{ handle: 'alice@x', backendRef: 'undefined' }`. `user_id: null` -> `'null'`; `user_id: {}` -> `'[object Object]'`; `user_id: [1,2]` -> `'1,2'`; `user_id: 1.5` -> `'1.5'`. The README states only two outcomes — the Zulip `user_id`, or a degrade to `{ handle, backendRef: handle }` — and this is a third the docs do not admit; two different handles whose matches both lack `user_id` collide on the same `'undefined'` backendRef. Traced, not reproduced: `is_active: 'false'` (a string, or `0`) is `!== false`, so a deactivated impostor stays in `active` and the JSDoc's promise that "a deactivated-only match degrades to the string convention" does not hold against a server that spells the flag any other way.
remediation: Filter `active` on a usable identifier before any matching, so an unusable record can neither answer nor consume the exactly-one slot: `const active = members.filter((u) => u?.is_active !== false && typeof u?.user_id === 'number' && Number.isSafeInteger(u.user_id) && u.user_id > 0)` — the same predicate `zulipToMessage` already applies to a message `id` (wire.ts:77). Leave `is_active !== false` as the polarity (an older server that omits the field must still resolve) but consider narrowing it to `u?.is_active !== false && u?.is_active !== 'false'` only if a real server is ever seen to stringify it; do not tighten to `=== true`.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a server-controlled record read by a seam call is trusted against its declared wire type'. untrusted-payload.test.ts's own docstring already names the right generator — "the cross product of every field a server controls and every shape the declaration says it cannot hold, so a field added to the wire type meets the whole hazard list by adding one name" — but its FIELDS list only covers `ZulipMessage`. Widen it to iterate the wire types themselves: for each of `ZulipMessage`, `RealmMember` and `EventsResponse`, cross every declared field with the existing HAZARDS array and drive it through the seam call that reads it (`fetchRecent`/push loop, `resolveIdentity`, the events loop), asserting a well-formed result — for `resolveIdentity` that means `backendRef` is either a positive-integer string or exactly the handle, never `'undefined'`, `'null'`, `'[object Object]'` or a comma-joined array.

summary: `occurrences(name)` counts raw `\bname\b` matches across every source and every test file — comments included — and `'exports no name the package never uses'` fails only when that count is `< 2`. The declaration line itself is occurrence #1, so a single `{@link Name}` in the symbol's own JSDoc is occurrence #2 and the dead export passes. This is CLAUDE.md's named 'lint with a hole' failure mode, in the file whose whole purpose is keeping the published surface enumerable. The same textual test defeats the sibling checks: `'the entry publishes only names a test consumes'` uses `new RegExp(\`\\b${name}\\b\`).test(testSources)`, so a name mentioned once in any test file's prose comment counts as consumed, and `'binds no import name the rest of the file never references'` tests against a body from which only import STATEMENTS were stripped, so an import referenced solely by a `{@link}` reads as used.
remediation: Strip comments before counting. Add `const code = (s) => s.replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, '').replace(/^\s*\/\/.*$/gm, '')` and apply it in the `sources`/`testSources` maps at lines 32-36, so `occurrences`, the entry-consumer regex and the unused-import body all read code only. Additionally require the count to include at least one occurrence OUTSIDE the declaring file, so a symbol used only by its own module cannot claim an export.

That is a table over evasion SHAPES rather than one more assertion about today's symbol list, and it catches the next scanner that forgets comments are not code.

failure: An operator reads the README, sees handles resolve to a Zulip user_id, and provisions handle `ops-lead` (not an email address). Any realm member sets their Zulip display name to `ops-lead`; `resolveIdentity('ops-lead')` now returns `{ handle: 'ops-lead', backendRef: '<their user_id>' }` — an unambiguous single match, so the uniqueness guard does not fire. summary: `scheduleReconnect`'s timer dials unconditionally and only THEN assigns `this.ready`, so it never notices a dial another caller already started. `chargeDialAttempt` sets `nextDialAt = Date.now() + wait` and the `setTimeout(..., wait)` is armed a moment later, so the wall clock always crosses `nextDialAt` strictly before the timer can fire. Any `ensureUp()` landing in that window (core's 250 ms long-poll fallback, or a blocking `fetchRecent`) sees `ready === undefined` and `wait <= 0`, dials, and the ladder timer then dials a SECOND socket on top of it — two IDENTIFYs charged for one rung of the ladder that exists solely to ration the 1000/24h per-token quota whose penalty is a bot-token reset. The method's own comment claims the opposite ("a re-entrant caller (core's 250 ms long-poll fallback) cannot open a second socket alongside this one").
failure: Reproduced with a 20-line concrete subclass of `GatewayLadder` (counting dials, no `ws`): schedule a reconnect after a READY socket drops (jitter pinned to 0 ⇒ wait = 1000 ms), advance the system clock 1000 ms WITHOUT firing timers, call `ensureUp()` → dial #1; then fire the timer → dial #2. Observed `dials === 2`, expected 1. Second socket also installs itself as `this.ws`, orphaning the first (which is only closed on its next inbound frame) — and the orphan already spent its IDENTIFY.
remediation: In `GatewayLadder.ensureUp`, refuse to dial while the ladder owns the next dial: inside `if (this.ready === undefined)`, add `if (this.reconnectTimer !== undefined) throw new Error('Discord gateway dial refused: the reconnect ladder already owns the next dial');` before the `nextDialAt` check. Do NOT instead guard the timer body with `if (this.ready !== undefined) return;` — after a READY socket drops non-terminally the close handler leaves `this.ready` as a STALE RESOLVED promise, so that guard would stop the ladder reconnecting at all.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any ladder path that opens a socket without going through the one budget. Parameterize a table over (who initiates: ensureUp / reconnect timer / close handler) × (arrival offset relative to nextDialAt: -1 ms, 0, +1 ms, +50 ms) × (previous socket reached READY: yes/no), asserting `dials` after fully draining timers equals the number of ladder RUNGS charged (`reconnectAttempts` delta), not merely that it is bounded. Existing `gateway-budget.test.ts` 'Discord IDENTIFY budget, whoever dials' and gateway-reconnect.test.ts:722 'sustained flapping stays under QUOTA_PER_DAY' are too narrow: both drive time forward only through `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, which fires the reconnect timer at exactly nextDialAt and therefore can never open the lateness window. The generator must move the clock independently of the timer queue (`vi.setSystemTime`).

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.reconnectTimer`, already the sole backing of the public `get reconnectPending()`, and `DiscordPlugin.subscribe`'s existing catch branch: `const ladder = this.gateway.reconnectPending ? 'the reconnect ladder is retrying' : 'no reconnect is scheduled'` — which prints the accurate message for the newly-thrown case. `fetchRecent`'s `try { await withDeadline(this.gateway.ensureUp(), blockMs) } catch { /* no socket → skip the wait */ }` already swallows it.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: an `ensureUp()` arriving after `nextDialAt` has passed but before the pending reconnect timer has fired — today it dials, now it throws a transient error and the ladder's own dial lands milliseconds later. Every other state is unchanged, because in that state `nextDialAt` is already in the future and `ensureUp` already threw 'backing off for another Xms'.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied this exact edit and ran the whole package suite: 1020 passed, and the only failure was my own scratch repro's intermediate assertion (`expect(l.dials).toBe(1)` right after the re-entrant call), which was written to pin the buggy behaviour. The repro's terminal assertion (total dials == 1) passes with the fix.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the double-dial. What stays broken if applied while the underlying shape remains: `this.ready` is still a stale resolved memo after a non-terminal close, so `ensureUp()` continues to resolve immediately on a dead socket — correct today only because `isLive()` is checked separately in the long-poll and `subscribe` does not care. Anyone who later removes the `isLive()` check gets a long-poll parking its whole budget on a dead socket.
remediationCheck.interleavings: (1) ensureUp at t=nextDialAt-ε → throws 'backing off', timer dials at t_fire: one dial. (2) ensureUp at t∈[nextDialAt, t_fire) → NOW throws on the new guard, timer dials: one dial (today: two). (3) two concurrent ensureUp callers in that window → both hit the new guard, neither dials. (4) ensureUp after the timer has fired and cleared `reconnectTimer` → `this.ready` is the timer's in-flight dial, so the memo path is taken: one dial. (5) `stop()`/`restart()` racing the guard → `stop()` clears `reconnectTimer` first, so a subsequent ensureUp dials normally under the fresh epoch.

summary: `newestWindow` builds `limit=${size}&before=${before}` with NO encoding, where `before` is `walked.at(-1)?.id` — a message id taken verbatim from the provider's response body. `hasUsableId` accepts any non-empty string, so the id is never constrained to digits. The sibling `windowSince` on line 43 does encode (`after=${encodeURIComponent(last ?? since)}`), so this is a one-sided hole in an otherwise deliberate defence. The threat is in scope for this package by its own choice: README line 58 says a plaintext `http://` `api_url` to a remote host is warned about and NOT refused, so a MITM on that path is an acknowledged deployment.
failure:
Reproduced against test/fake-discord.ts: seed a channel, `injectFault({status:200, rawBody: <a full 100-record page whose OLDEST record has id '900&limit=1&after=0'>})`, then `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 150})`. The fake logged the two requests it received:
  /api/v10/channels/900001/messages?limit=100
  /api/v10/channels/900001/messages?limit=50&before=900&limit=1&after=0
The provider-controlled id smuggled a duplicate `limit` and an injected `after` into the plugin's own paging query — on real Discord that silently returns a different window (or a 400), so the backward walk's contract ("a larger limit is not answered with a truncated head whose cursor already sits past everything older than it") is decided by response data rather than by the plugin.
remediation: `before === undefined ? \`limit=${size}\` : \`limit=${size}&before=${encodeURIComponent(before)}\`` — matching the `after=` arm one function below. Better still, build both query strings with `URLSearchParams` so neither arm can drift again, and tighten `hasUsableId` to require `/^\d+$/` (a Discord snowflake is decimal) so a non-routable id is refused at the seam boundary instead of at each interpolation site.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a provider-supplied string reaching a request URL without encoding. Widen `rest-contract.test.ts`'s 'a topic that tries to reshape the provider request' table from one axis (hostile TOPIC) to three (hostile topic × hostile CURSOR passed as `since` × hostile provider-returned `id` injected via `injectFault` on page 0 of a multi-page walk), and strengthen `expectStayedOnRoute`: its `CHANNEL_ROUTE` regex today ends in `(\?[^#]*)?$`, which accepts ANY query string, so it cannot see query injection at all. Assert instead that `new URLSearchParams(route.search)` has exactly the expected keys with exactly one value each, and that each decoded value equals what the plugin intended. Reuse the same HOSTILE_IDS strings ('x?limit=1', 'x&after=0', 'x#frag', 'x%2F') so the generator also covers inputs I did not try.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing new — `encodeURIComponent` is already imported-free (global) and is the exact call `windowSince` makes on line 43 for the symmetric anchor.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at the type level; a provider id containing reserved characters is now percent-encoded rather than interpreted, so such a page walk asks Discord for `before=<the literal id>` and gets a 400 or an empty window instead of a silently different one.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied the encodeURIComponent edit and ran the whole package suite: 18 files / 1019 tests passed. Every real and fake id in this package is decimal, so encoding is a no-op on the happy path.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It closes the injection at this one site. What stays broken: `hasUsableId` still lets a non-snowflake id cross the seam as `backendMsgId` AND `cursor`, so core persists it and hands it back as `since` on the next call — where it is encoded, hence harmless, but it is still a cursor no Discord route can resolve, which reads to the operator as a permanently empty topic rather than as a refused page. That is why the second half of the remediation (anchor `hasUsableId` on `/^\d+$/`) matters.

Worse, the table's own `CHANNEL_ROUTE` regex ends `(\?[^#]*)?$` — it accepts any query string — so even if a cursor row existed, the assertion could not see query-string injection.

summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then calls `this.runFetch({...args, since: floor})`. Every settled exit is covered (`wake()` on a satisfied re-query, `await wait` on an empty one, `stop()`'s drain on disconnect, the socket-loss drain) EXCEPT a rejection: if the re-query throws — any `ok:false` that is not an absence code, a shape error, a repeated page cursor, a walk over MAX_HISTORY_PAGES — the exception unwinds past both `wake()` and `await wait`, so the waiter stays registered in `link.waiters` with a live timer, and every live event on that channel iterates it, until its own timer fires up to one ladder rung (≤5 s) later. `harness.ts`'s `parkedWaiters` doc names four exits and omits this fifth, and `withBlocking`'s guard only wraps calls that resolve.
failure: With `greet:'silent'` and `fake.onHit('conversations.history', hit => { if (hit >= 1) fake.failMethod('conversations.history','internal_error') })`, `await plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since: asCursor('0'), limit: 10, blockMs: 5000})` rejects with `Slack conversations.history → internal_error` and `parkedWaiters(plugin)` is 1 immediately after the call settles (expected 0). Reproduced.
remediation: In the ladder body, wrap only the re-query so a throw drains its own waiter before propagating: `let requeried; try { requeried = await this.runFetch({ ...args, since: floor }); } catch (e) { wake(); throw e; }`. Use a catch, NOT a finally — a `finally { wake() }` would fire before `await wait` on the normal empty-page path and turn the capped ladder into a hot re-query spin.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a registered resource whose release is on the success path only'. Add REJECTION as an explicit exit axis to the blocking-fetch table: parameterize over {woken, timed out, disconnected mid-park, socket lost, re-query rejects} × {a 4xx-shaped ok:false, a SlackShapeError, a repeated page cursor} and assert `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0` for every one, with the call captured via `capture()` so a rejection is a row failure rather than an unhandled rejection. Change `withBlocking` so its post-condition runs for rejected calls too (wrap `fn` in try/finally), which is what let this exit escape the existing guard.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The `wake` half of the handle `this.link.armWaiter(...)` already returns, and `Waiter.wake`'s `if (done) return;` idempotence guard in src/link.ts:157 — so waking here cannot double-resolve a waiter that a concurrent `drainWaiters()` already released.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no input classification changes; the same call still rejects with the same error.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked blocking-fetch.test.ts's two `parkedWaiters(...)===0` assertions (lines 67 and 437) and the six-row degradation table; all of them drive calls that RESOLVE, so none observes the rejecting path at all.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If it were not applied, the leak is still self-healing: the waiter's own `setTimeout(waiter.wake, min(remaining, rung))` fires within ≤ MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS and deregisters it, and `disconnect()` drains it sooner. So this is a bounded leak of one timer plus a spurious wake of an already-dead call, not a hang — which is why it is a suggestion. What stays broken without it is the invariant `parkedWaiters` was written to state, and therefore the ability of any future test to use that probe as a settled-call post-condition.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers blocking on the same channel, one rejecting: caller A rejects and calls its own `wake()`, which deletes only A's waiter from the channel's Set (and the Set itself only when it empties), leaving B's untouched. A live event arriving between the throw and the `wake()` iterates a snapshot `[...waiting]` and may wake A's waiter first — harmless, since `wake` is idempotent and A's `await wait` is already unreachable. A concurrent `stop()` drains both and clears the map; the later `wake()` finds no Set and returns after `resolveWait()`.

summary: seam.ts states ascending-cursor handler invocation as a plugin guarantee, and src/link.ts's own class comment concedes the plugin suspends it during a `disconnect: warning` rotation ('it rests on ONE connection feeding a channel, which a rotation deliberately suspends'). During the grace both sockets are established and `routeEnvelope` invokes handlers from either — it never checks `this.ws === ws` for an `events_api` envelope — so for up to `rotation_grace_ms` (default 10 000 ms) the live path can deliver a channel's events out of ts order. The README's only mention of that window is the config comment 'how long a rotated-out socket may stay open once replaced', which describes a connection count, not a relaxed ordering guarantee. No test grades ordering across a rotation either: connection-lifecycle.test.ts's rotation rows assert socket counts and that the replacement carries the stream, never the order of what is delivered.
failure: Subscribe to a mapped topic, push `{type:'disconnect', reason:'warning'}`, wait for two live sockets, then have Slack route event ts=…002 to the replacement and ts=…001 to the still-open old socket. The handler is invoked with …002 before …001 — a descending pair on a seam that declares ascending order — and an operator reading the README has no way to predict it.
remediation: Document it: add a sentence to the README's rotation/`rotation_grace_ms` text stating that a rotation deliberately runs two connections for up to `rotation_grace_ms`, that Slack routes each payload to exactly one of them, and that live-path ordering is therefore not guaranteed inside that window — catch-up (`fetchRecent` cursor order) is the ordered path. The behavioural alternative — after the replacement greets, keep the old socket ACKING but stop invoking route handlers from it (gate the `events_api` arm of `routeEnvelope` on `this.ws === ws`) — restores single-source ordering but converts a gapless rotation into live-push loss for that window, repaired only on the next catch-up; do not take it without deciding that trade explicitly.

Add a rotation-ordering row to connection-lifecycle.test.ts driven from the fake's two-socket state: subscribe, push the warning, wait for `liveSockets===2`, then push a descending-ts pair across the two sockets and assert the handler order the package COMMITS to. Pair it with a README-parity test in the style of documented-scopes.test.ts — key the assertion off the exported `DEFAULT_ROTATION_GRACE_MS` and require the README paragraph to name both the constant and the ordering caveat — so a future relaxation of any other guarantee has to move the prose with it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing in the code path for the documentation fix. The behavioural alternative would rely on `this.ws` already being reassigned to the replacement inside `openSocket` (src/link.ts:227) before the old socket's grace elapses, which the rotation path does guarantee: `routeEnvelope`'s warning arm sets `this.wsReady = undefined` and calls `reconnect()`, and only `openSocket` assigns `this.ws`.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Documentation fix: none. Behavioural alternative: every `events_api` envelope arriving on a rotated-out socket is no longer delivered to a subscribe handler (it is still acked).
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Documentation fix: none found — no test asserts the absence of such a sentence, and documented-scopes.test.ts's README scans are anchored on the scope table and the rate-limit paragraph. Anything above the seam that genuinely requires ascending live delivery is still exposed for `rotation_grace_ms` per rotation; only the behavioural alternative closes that, at the cost of live-push loss in the same window.

Note this is a repo-wide pattern, not slack-only — bridge-discord (`@types/ws`) and bridge-postgres (`@types/pg`) have the identical shape — so fixing it here alone leaves the class open.

summary: `StoreFile.replace()` calls `writeSync(fd, text)` once and ignores the byte count it returns. `fs.writeSync` performs a single `write(2)` and does NOT loop (unlike `appendFileSync`/`writeFileSync`, whose looping this package already relies on — see store-torn-write.test.ts's own comment). failure: Reproduced standalone: `StoreFile.replace(journal)` with a 46913-byte journal (400 records) under an 8192-byte write ceiling. `replace` threw NOTHING; the store file was published at 8192 bytes holding 71 whole records plus a torn fragment, not newline-terminated. On the next load the fragment is dropped, `#seq 400 400` states intact=400 against onDisk=71, so the store mints a fresh epoch and refuses every outstanding cursor — 329 observed messages gone, with no Bot API history endpoint that could put them back. summary: `fetchOnce` calls `AbortSignal.timeout(budgetMs)` before the `try`, with no validation. Node requires an integer in [0, 4294967295], so a fractional or oversized budget throws a raw `RangeError` that bypasses the label/redact/sanitize envelope this module's own test file asserts nothing leaves without. `budgetMs` is `deadlineMs - (now() - started)`, so BOTH documented knobs reach it: `deadlineMs` (documented with no integer constraint) and `now` (documented only as "Injectable clock, for tests").
failure: Reproduced in-repo against the real module. `fetchWithRetry(url, {}, { label: 'L', isStopped: () => false, deadlineMs: 100.5 })` -> rejects with `RangeError: The value of "delay" is out of range. It must be an integer. Received 100.5` — no `L → ` prefix, no redaction of the credential-bearing URL, and `statusOf(err) === undefined`. Worse, `{ label:'L', isStopped:()=>false, now: () => performance.now() }` with the DEFAULT deadline -> `RangeError … Received 29999.994656` on the very first attempt, i.e. the obvious high-resolution reading of the documented `now` option makes every call fail. `deadlineMs: 5_000_000_000` -> `RangeError … must be >= 0 && <= 4294967295`. And `deadlineMs: 3_000_000_000` (under 2^32, over 2^31) is silently clamped by Node's timer to 1 ms with a `TimeoutOverflowWarning`, aborting the request immediately.
remediation: In `fetchWithRetry`, validate the caller's bounds once, up front, and reject inside the envelope: if `!Number.isFinite(opts.deadlineMs ?? DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS)` or it is <= 0, throw `new LabelledError(`${opts.label} → deadlineMs must be a positive finite number of milliseconds`, undefined)`. In `fetchOnce`, arm the signal from a normalized figure rather than the raw one: `AbortSignal.timeout(Math.min(Math.trunc(budgetMs), 2 ** 31 - 1))` — the truncation makes a sub-millisecond clock (`performance.now`) harmless, and the ceiling stops Node's 32-bit timer overflow turning a long deadline into an instant abort.

Widen it mechanically rather than by list: derive the option names from `declaredOptions()` (already parsed in `package-contract.test.ts`) so a future numeric option arrives as rows. The existing `honours the deadline against %s` rows are too narrow — every one passes an integer literal, and `now:` is only ever `(clock += 1)`.

summary: The KNOWN_FORKS registry is a genuinely good instrument, but it grades only the EXISTENCE of a fork, never its behaviour - so a recorded fork may silently diverge from the shared implementation forever, and two of its three rows record duplication the table itself calls costless. bridge-nats:delay and bridge-redis:delay are recorded with the reason 'a duplicate with no obstruction at all: importing delay from here is a one-line change in that package, which owns it' - a permanently-green entry whose stated remediation is one line (packages/bridge-nats/src/jetstream.ts:11 and packages/bridge-redis/src/read-loop.ts:21 are byte-equivalent to packages/bridge-net-util/src/timing.ts:2 modulo the resolver's parameter name). More seriously, bridge-discord:plaintextRemoteOrigin (packages/bridge-discord/src/creds.ts:37) fails in the OPPOSITE DIRECTION from the shared one, and the registry cannot tell.
failure: net-util's plaintext.ts classifies by an allowlist of SECURE schemes and its comment states the rule: 'Keep the set on the SECURE side, so that a scheme this classifier has never met ... is warned about rather than passed'; its own test table carries the row ['x-vendor-stream', true] to pin that direction. bridge-discord's recorded fork classifies by a DENYLIST - PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES = new Map([['http:', 'https://'], ['ws:', 'wss://']]) - so plaintextRemoteOrigin('x-vendor-stream://evil.example.com') returns undefined (no warning) where the shared one returns the origin. Input -> wrong output: backend_config.gateway_url = 'x-vendor-stream://evil.example.com' produces no SECURITY line from packages/bridge-discord/src/session.ts:60, while the identical value through net-util warns. Both registry rows still pass: forks() only checks the NAME collides, and classifiers() only checks a loopback literal is not decided locally - and discord's fork delegates isLoopbackHost, so it is exempt from that scan too.
remediation: Retire the two delay rows by changing one import line in packages/bridge-nats/src/jetstream.ts and packages/bridge-redis/src/read-loop.ts (both packages already depend on @sharptrick/parley-net-util). For the discord fork, do what its own recorded reason says retires it: widen net-util's plaintextRemoteOrigin to return { origin, secure } | undefined (or add a sibling secureSchemeFor(protocol)), delete packages/bridge-discord/src/creds.ts:37 and import the shared one - which also flips discord onto the fail-safe direction.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a recorded-debt registry that pins existence but not behaviour, so a fork may drift from the thing it forked. Add to plaintext-classifier.test.ts a row set that runs each RECORDED fork against the shared implementation's own parameter table: for bridge-discord:plaintextRemoteOrigin, import the fork and assert fork(url) === undefined iff plaintextRemoteOrigin(url) === undefined across the existing SCHEMES x HOSTS cross-product (a fork returning a richer type is compared on its undefined-ness, the security-relevant bit). Add a second row asserting that any KNOWN_FORKS entry whose recorded reason contains 'no obstruction' fails the table - a debt with no obstruction is not a debt, it is an unmade edit.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: packages/bridge-net-util/test/plaintext-classifier.test.ts 'every recorded fork still exists, so the table cannot outlive the debt' would fail once the forks are deleted without also removing their KNOWN_FORKS rows - that coupling is intended. I grepped packages/bridge-discord/test/*.ts for assertions on the fork's { origin, secure } shape; they assert on the warning STRING via plaintextCredentialRisks, which the widened shared return keeps buildable.

summary: The `rotating` WeakSet ('one rotation per socket') appears to be unreachable-as-necessary, dominated by the two conditions beside it. `reconnect()` is an async function whose `if (this.reconnecting) return; this.reconnecting = true;` prologue runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, so by the time `routeEnvelope`'s warning arm returns, `reconnecting` is already true — a burst of warnings in the same tick is stopped by `this.reconnecting`. And `reconnecting` only returns to false in `reconnect()`'s `finally`, which is reached after `ensureSocket()` succeeded, i.e. after `openSocket` has reassigned `this.ws` to the replacement — at which point a further warning on the old socket is stopped by `this.ws !== ws`. I removed the `rotating.has(ws)` term and the full 880-test suite stayed green, which is consistent with it grading nothing.
failure: Not a runtime failure. `src/link.ts:65` (the WeakSet field + its JSDoc) and the `|| this.rotating.has(ws)` term plus `this.rotating.add(ws)` can all be deleted with the suite green — a guard carried as coverage that no interleaving in the fixture can distinguish.
remediation: Either delete `rotating` (field, JSDoc, add, and the disjunct), or keep it and add the interleaving test that shows what it catches — a second `disconnect: warning` on the SAME socket during a window where `reconnecting` has already returned to false but `this.ws` is still that socket. If no such window can be constructed, that is the answer.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a defensive guard no fixture can reach'. Rather than a test per guard, add a mutation gate to the package's own discipline: for each named single-socket/single-owner guard in link.ts (`reconnecting`, `rotating`, `this.ws !== ws`, `helloSeen`, the `session()` checks in `openSocket`/`ensureSocket`), a table-driven envelope-injection test that drives the specific interleaving each one claims to stop — pushing warnings and closes at chosen points relative to the replacement's `hello` via `fake.setGreet` and `fake.onHit` — so a guard that cannot be reached fails the table by having no row rather than by being silently green.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `reconnect()`'s prologue in src/link.ts:282-283 (`if (this.reconnecting) return; this.reconnecting = true;` — synchronous, before any await) and `openSocket`'s `this.ws = ws` at src/link.ts:227, which is the only assignment to `this.ws` other than `stop()`'s clear.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: Deletion accepts a second `disconnect: warning` on a socket that is still `this.ws` while no reconnect owner exists — if such a state is reachable, that warning would start a second rotation of the same socket.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the full 880-test suite with the `rotating.has(ws)` term removed and it was green; the two rotation tests (connection-lifecycle.test.ts:506 and :534) both push warnings sequentially, each landing on a NEW current socket, so neither exercises the term.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If `rotating` really is dominated, deleting it changes nothing at runtime and removes a line that reads as covered but is not. If it is NOT dominated — i.e. there is an interleaving I did not construct in which `reconnecting` is false while `this.ws === ws` after a rotation already started — deleting it reopens a second-rotation-per-socket path, which is why the remediation is stated as an either/or and this is marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The one I could not rule out: `reconnect()` returns (finally clears `reconnecting`) without `openSocket` having reassigned `this.ws`. That requires `ensureSocket()` to resolve off a memoized `wsReady` belonging to an older socket, which the warning arm's `this.wsReady = undefined` immediately before `reconnect()` appears to prevent — but I did not trace every path that can re-arm `wsReady` between those two statements.
